note.title: Case functions
note.overview: Recognise what each case does before memorising endings.
learningGoals: Name the core function of each of the six cases.
mustMemoriseRules: Nominative subject; vocative address; accusative object; genitive of; dative to or for; ablative by with or from.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — What is the main job of the ablative case?
workedExamples.why: The school sheet gives by with or from as the core job of the ablative.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — What is the main job of the accusative case?
workedExamples.why: The school sheet gives object as the core job of the accusative.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — What is the main job of the dative case?
workedExamples.why: The school sheet gives indirect object as the core job of the dative.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — What is the main job of the genitive case?
workedExamples.why: The school sheet gives of as the core job of the genitive.

workedExamples.prompt: TYPE THE ANSWER — What is the main job of the nominative case?
workedExamples.why: The school sheet gives subject as the core job of the nominative.

commonMistakes: Confusing dative to or for with genitive of.
Forgetting that vocative is direct address.
A familiar stem with the wrong case, number, person or tense ending is not correct.
detailedExplanation: Recognise what each case does before memorising endings.

Latin noun endings show the word's grammatical job as well as number. Identify the dictionary form and stem, decide the required case and number from the sentence, then select the ending. Translate the function, not simply the first familiar meaning.
examTips: Mark the finite verb first, then use noun endings to assign subject, object and recipient roles.
Normal Latin word order can vary; the case, number, gender, person and tense endings cannot.
For English to Latin, build each required form before arranging the sentence.
